title: Context-level Language Modeling by Learning Predictive Context Embeddings
claim: A chunk-level context predictor sits between a token encoder and decoder, predicting the next context embedding to improve next-token prediction.
layout: single vertical panel, bottom-to-top flow, color-coded chunks, feedback arrow on left
description: A single tall block diagram read from bottom to top. Input tokens x0–x11 sit at the bottom under a yellow Token Encoder bar. The encoder outputs hidden states h0–h11, grouped into three dashed, color-coded chunks (green, red, yellow) of four tokens each. A caption box says 'Mapping token-level embeddings into context embedding' and reduces each chunk to one context embedding c0, c1, c2. These feed a large blue Context Predictor block, which outputs the predicted next-context embeddings ĉ1, ĉ2, ĉ3, plus an initial c_init. A second caption box says 'Incorporating the predictive context embedding back into tokens'. The embeddings are merged into token groups h0–h11, and a black arrow loops up the left side to the group's start. An orange Token Decoder at the top outputs the predicted tokens x̂1–x̂12, colored to match their chunks. Color coding links tokens to chunks and contexts throughout.
caption: Scaling performance comparison across three dimensions: parameters, training tokens, and training FLOPs for GPT-2 and \MethodName-GPT2.
abstract: We propose ContextLM, a framework that implicitly learns multi-token prediction by augmenting standard pretraining with an intrinsic next-context prediction objective. ContextLM builds a language model on top of context embeddings that span multiple tokens, enabling better next-token prediction by predicting the next context. Our model is fully compatible with standard autoregressive, token-by-token evaluation paradigms (e.g., perplexity). Extensive experiments with GPT-2 and Pythia backbones (up to 1.5B parameters and 300B training tokens) reveal that ContextLM shifts the Pareto frontier of scaling laws, exhibiting superior efficiency in parameters, training tokens, and FLOPs. Our results show that ContextLM could already achieve the baseline perplexity using 39\% fewer parameters and demonstrates robust generalization improvements on extensive downstream tasks under equivalent parameter counts.
